\section{P1: weighted and Euclidean radii in the connection estimate
(Major)}\label{P1}

\subsection{Location and claim}
The relevant definitions are (4.1)--(4.5), pp.~22--23; the affected
statements are Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2, pp.~23--25. They feed directly into
(4.16)--(4.20) and the contradiction proving (1.19), p.~26. The weighted
semidistance and normal spheres are
\[
 d_F^*(v,w)=\inf_\gamma\int\sqrt{2F(\gamma)}|\gamma'|\dd t,\qquad
 N(p,r)=\{z:d_F^*(z,p)=r,\ P_{m_\pm}z=p\}.
\]
In (4.5), both normal spheres have \emph{weighted} radius $\delta_0$,
and $\kappa$ contains the additive correction $2\delta_0-c_F$.
Lemma 4.2 instead stops a curve when it exits the \emph{Euclidean}
tube $B_{\delta_0}(m_\pm)$.

\subsection{A counterexample to the stated lemmas}
Set $a=\delta_0=1/100$ and take two unit circles in $\R^2$,
\[
 m_-=\{(1+\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\},\qquad
 m_+=\{(4+\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\}.
\]
They are compact, connected, smooth and disjoint; $0\in m_-$,
$D=1$, and the $2a$-tubes have smooth nearest-point projections.
The closest pair is $p_-=(2,0)$, $p_+=(3,0)$.

Choose a monotone smooth $f$ satisfying the prescribed endpoint
conditions, with $a^2\leq f\leq2a^2$ in the intermediate interval.
For completeness, such a $C^\infty$ choice can be made explicitly.
For $0<z<1$, put
\[
 s(z)=\frac{e^{-1/z}}{e^{-1/z}+e^{-1/(1-z)}},\quad
 b(z)=e^{-1/[z(1-z)]},\quad B=\int_0^1b(z)\dd z,
 \quad w(z)=1-s(z)+\frac{b(z)}{2B}.
\]
Extend $s$ by $0,1$ and $b$ by zero at the endpoints. Symmetry gives
$\int_0^1s=1/2$, hence $\int_0^1w=1$; $w\geq0$, $w(0)=1$,
$w(1)=0$, and all derivatives needed for gluing are flat. Define
\[
 f(t)=a^2\left[1+\int_0^{(t-a^2)/a^2}w(z)\dd z\right]
       \quad(a^2<t<2a^2)
\]
and use $f(t)=t$ below and $f(t)=2a^2$ above.
Thus the example satisfies the potential hypotheses, including
smoothness of $F$ across the parts where the distance function has
a cut locus, because $f$ is already constant there.

Direct bounds on the defining integral give
\[
 2a-4\sqrt2\,a^2\leq c_F
 \leq 2a-(4-\sqrt2)a^2.
\]
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cfbounds}
 0.019434\leq c_F\leq0.0197415,\qquad a<c_F<2a.
\end{equation}
The displayed decimal bounds are certified by the rational enclosure
$1.414<\sqrt2<1.415$, not by floating-point quadrature.

On the closest segment, write $z(q)=(2+q,0)$, $0\leq q\leq1$, and
\[
 S(q)=\int_0^q\sqrt{2f(\min\{r,1-r\}^2)}\dd r.
\]
Then $S(0)=0$, $S(1)=c_F$, and
$d_F^*(z(q),p_-)=S(q)$,
$d_F^*(z(q),p_+)=c_F-S(q)$.
Here is an independent justification of the lower bounds implicit in
these equalities. Put $h(x)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x_1-2\}\}$.
For $2\leq x_1\leq3$, the distance to the two circles is at least
$\min\{h(x),1-h(x)\}$. Monotonicity of the chosen $f$ therefore gives
$|\nabla(S\circ h)|\leq\sqrt{2F}$ almost everywhere.
Integrating this calibration along any path gives the lower bound;
the straight segment attains it. This also excludes shortcuts along
the zero-cost wells.

Because $a<c_F$, the spheres $N(p_\pm,a)$ are nonempty, with explicit
points on this segment. Their distance is finite and nonnegative.
For every sufficiently small $\rho\geq0$, the definition (4.5) therefore
implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kappapos}
 \kappa(p_+,p_-,\rho)\geq2a-c_F
 \geq \frac{517}{2000000}>0.
\end{equation}
At $\rho=0$ this contradicts the zero-value conclusion of Lemma 4.1
for the minimal pair $(p_+,p_-)$.

It also contradicts Lemma 4.2 itself. Let $[local archive path omitted],1)$ be the
increasing optimal profile
\[
 Q'=\sqrt{2f(\min\{Q,1-Q\}^2)},\qquad Q(-\infty)=0,\quad Q(+\infty)=1,
\]
and set $\gamma(\tau)=z(Q(\tau/\eps))$ on a fixed interval $[-h,h]$.
For small $\eps$, $\gamma(\pm h)\in B_a(m_\pm)$, so (4.7) holds.
Along this curve $d_F(\gamma)=S(Q)$, and pointwise
\[
 \frac12|\gamma'|^2+\frac{F(\gamma)}{\eps^2}
       -\frac{(d_F\circ\gamma)'}{\eps}=0.
\]
For every fixed $0<\rho<\rho_0$, the claimed lower bound (4.8) is
strictly positive by \eqref{eq:kappapos}, whereas its left side is zero.
This is an exact counterexample, with no numerical solution of the
author's PDE or code.

\subsection{Scope of a possible smallness interpretation}
The proof of Lemma 3.4 mentions $\delta_0\ll c_F$ on p.~18.
The unit-gap example does not satisfy that extra informal relation.
It does satisfy the explicitly stated hypotheses (1.3)--(1.6).
Because the same $\delta_0$ fixes the height of the plateau in $f$,
shrinking $\delta_0$ in this example does not make
$\delta_0/c_F$ tend to zero. Thus this relation cannot silently be
obtained from the written assumptions by making the tube thinner.

There is also a separate defect even under an arbitrarily strong
relation $\delta_0\ll c_F$. Move the second circle's center to
$(L+3,0)$, so that $D=L$ can be as large as desired. Then
$c_F\sim2aL$, but an actual Euclidean tube exit at distance $a$ has
weighted distance
\[
 r_a=\int_0^a\sqrt2\,r\dd r=\frac{a^2}{\sqrt2}\neq a.
\]
After correcting the exit-time notation, the optimal straight profile
has $P_m\gamma(t_+)=P_m\gamma(h)=p_+$ and
$\gamma(t_+)\notin N(\overline B_\rho(p_+)\cap m_+,a)$.
Case (1) on p.~25 would nevertheless force
$|P_m\gamma(t_+)-P_m\gamma(h)|\geq C_1\rho>0$.
This is false even when $a/c_F$ is arbitrarily small.

Two additional local errors are part of this same proof failure.
The printed infimum defining $t_-$ on p.~24 equals $-h$ rather than
the intended first exit; the printed supremum defining $t_+$ equals
$h$ rather than the last entrance. The infimum and supremum must be
interchanged. Also, the upper bound ending
$d_F^*(N_+,N_-)\leq c_F-2\delta_0+\beta$ on p.~24 does not imply
the asserted equality $\kappa=\beta>0$. The first equality for $I_0$
in case (3), p.~25, is in general a lower bound obtained by
Cauchy--Schwarz.

\subsection{Impact and repair boundary}
The estimate used to force minimal-pair traces is not established.
This is a Major issue because (1.19) is a principal advertised
conclusion. The counterexample concerns the auxiliary connection
lemma, not an actual limiting pair violating Theorem 1.1.

A consistent reconstruction must use a geometric tube radius $r$
and the distinct weighted radius
$r_F=\int_0^r\sqrt{2f(s^2)}\dd s$.
The normal spheres and additive correction must then use $r_F$ and
$2r_F$, while the exit times use the Euclidean tube of radius $r$.
The strict gap for nonminimal endpoint pairs, its compactness and
continuity properties, and the resulting curve estimate still require
a complete proof. Merely replacing one occurrence of $\delta_0$ does
not verify this repair. The precise minimal-connection equality case
in Lin--Pan--Wang \cite{LPW}, Section 2, is relevant, but does not
by itself validate the printed $\kappa$ argument.

\section{P2: the collar construction does not preserve general
$H^1$ data (Major)}\label{P2}

\subsection{Location}
On p.~26, (5.1) calls $\Psi_\delta^\pm$ global $C^1$
diffeomorphisms, while requiring $\Psi_\delta^\pm=P_{\Sigma_0}$
on the entire open collar $B_\delta(\Sigma_0)$.
On p.~27, (5.2) asserts that
$u_0^\pm=u_{\pm}^{\rm in}\circ\Psi_\delta^\pm$ belongs to $H^1$,
and (5.10) uses these extensions to define $u_\eps^{\rm in}$.

Already at the smooth geometric level, $DP_{\Sigma_0}$ has rank
$d-1$ in the collar. Such a map is not a diffeomorphism between
$d$-dimensional domains. The more substantial defect remains even
if the map is renamed a collapsing extension.

\subsection{Admissible trace counterexample}
Take $\Omega=B_3(0)\subset\R^2$ and $\Sigma_0=S^1$, with
$\Omega_0^+=B_1(0)$ and $\Omega_0^-=B_3(0)\setminus\overline B_1(0)$.
A short smooth mean curvature evolution exists, and the separation
from the outer boundary meets the geometric hypothesis for small
$\delta_0$. In target space $\R^3$, take the parallel circles
\[
 m_-=\{(1-\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)\},\qquad
 m_+=m_-+(0,0,D),\quad D>0.
\]
They satisfy all well hypotheses, including $0\in m_-$, and pairs
at the same angle have exactly the minimal distance $D$.

Let
\[
 a(\theta)=c\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{-3j/4}\sin(2^j\theta),
 \qquad c=\frac1{100}.
\]
The series converges absolutely and uniformly and has
$|a|<\pi/8$. Its Sobolev seminorms satisfy
\[
 \sum_j 2^j\,2^{-3j/2}<\infty,\qquad
 \sum_j 2^{2j}\,2^{-3j/2}=\infty.
\]
Thus $a\in H^{1/2}(S^1)\cap C(S^1)$ but $a\notin H^1(S^1)$.
This is a divergence proof, not an inference from finitely many
sampled Fourier modes.

Let $a_+$ be the harmonic extension to the disk, and let $a_-$
be the harmonic extension to the annulus with inner boundary value
$a$ and outer boundary value zero. The Fourier energy formulas, or
the $H^{1/2}$ trace theorem, give $a_\pm\in H^1$.
The maximum principle keeps their values in $(-\pi/8,\pi/8)$.
Define
\[
 u_-^{\rm in}=(1-\cos a_-,\sin a_-,0),\qquad
 u_+^{\rm in}=(1-\cos a_+,\sin a_+,D).
\]
These are bounded $H^1$ well-valued maps. The outer boundary value
is the smooth constant zero, and their interface traces have
distance exactly $D$. In particular, they satisfy the full
minimal-pair assumption (1.23), not merely separate phase membership.

On the collar, (5.1)--(5.2) give the first two coordinates
\[
 (1-\cos a(\theta),\sin a(\theta)),
\]
constant in the normal coordinate. This is not an $H^1$ map on
any positive-width annulus. If it were, its second component would
be $H^1$ there, and composition with the Lipschitz function
$\arcsin$ on its range would give the constant normal extension
of $a$ in $H^1$. Integration in the normal variable would imply
$a\in H^1(S^1)$, a contradiction.

The failure persists in the actual final construction (5.10).
The two extended maps have identical first two coordinates and
differ only in the third coordinate. Therefore interpolation by
$S_\eps$ changes only that third coordinate. The non-$H^1$ first
two coordinates remain unchanged for every $\eps$.
The constructed $u_\eps^{\rm in}$ is consequently not in $H^1$.

\subsection{Impact and repair boundary}
This disproves the claimed construction for admissible inputs of
Theorem 1.2. It does not prove that no other preparation sequence
exists. A valid proof needs a Sobolev-compatible gluing construction
that preserves the minimal-pair constraint and the $O(\eps)$
modulated-energy bound, possibly with smoothing scales depending
on $\eps$. Alternatively, stronger tangential trace regularity
would change the theorem's stated scope.
Renaming $\Psi_\delta^\pm$, or citing a trace theorem that supplies
only $H^{1/2}$ traces, does not repair the argument.
The initial construction in the separately checked Laux--Liu
preprint \cite{LL} starts with a global $H^1$ map and does not
supply this missing extension for arbitrary pairs of bulk maps.

retained_calculation.analytic_conclusion: Full H^(1/2) sum is geometric and finite; the H^1 sum diverges. Constant normal extension retains this non-H^1 tangential trace on a positive-width collar.

\subsection{P3: insufficient SBV jump hypothesis (Minor)}\label{P3}

\textbf{Location.}
Propositions 2.2 and 2.3, p.~6, especially (2.2); application in
Theorem 3.6, p.~22.

\textbf{Counterexample.}
On $(0,1)$, let $\mu_j$ put mass $2^{-j}$ at the midpoint of
each of the $2^j$ surviving intervals in the $j$th middle-third
Cantor construction, and let $v_j(x)=\mu_j((0,x])$.
Each $v_j$ is a step function in $\SBV$, $0\leq v_j\leq1$,
$\nabla^a v_j=0$, and
\[
 \int_{J_{v_j}}|v_j^+-v_j^-|\dd\Ha^0=1.
\]
Choose $\varphi(t)=t^2$, which satisfies all conditions in
Proposition 2.2. The distribution functions converge uniformly
to the continuous Cantor function $v$, and their derivative
measures converge weakly to Cantor measure. Thus $v_j\to v$
weakly star in $BV$, but $D^cv\neq0$ and $v\notin\SBV$.
Every assumption in both stated propositions is met.

\textbf{Impact and correction.}
A linear jump-amplitude cost does not exclude a Cantor part.
An unweighted uniform bound on jump-set measure, together with
the other displayed bounds, is sufficient in the actual
application. More generally, a jump cost $\vartheta$ with
$\vartheta(s)/s\to\infty$ as $s\downarrow0$ supplies the missing
small-jump control; see the precise primary theorem
\cite{AM}, Theorem 1.4 and Proposition 2.5.
Theorem 3.6 already invokes the area bound (3.28a), the gradient
bound (3.29b), and bounded values. Replacing the quoted
compactness theorem by its correct form is therefore a bounded
repair, which is why this is Minor despite the false preliminary
statements.

retained_calculation.analytic_conclusion: The jump-amplitude sum is one and the approximate gradient is zero, while the continuous uniform limit has a nonzero Cantor derivative.

\subsection{P4: incompatible gradient conventions and a well sign
(Minor)}\label{P4}

\textbf{Location.}
The plus-well case of (2.21), p.~8; the unconditional definition
(2.35) and the classical-coincidence assertion in Lemma 2.7,
p.~11; the convention immediately below (2.40), p.~12; and
(2.41).

At a differentiability point, (2.35) projects the classical
gradient of $d_F$ onto
\[
 V=\operatorname{span}\{\partial_tu_\eps,\partial_1u_\eps,
                  \ldots,\partial_du_\eps\}.
\]
Such a projection need not equal the full classical gradient.
This is not merely a possible choice of arbitrary jets:
the following exact smooth solution of (1.7) demonstrates it.

Use $\Omega=(0,\pi)$ and two unit circles in the first two
coordinates of $\R^5$, centered at $(1,0)$ and $(5,0)$; their
last three coordinates are zero. Set $g=0$, $\delta_0=0.01$,
$\eps=0.1$, $K=100$, $t_*=K^{-2}$, and
$A=\delta_0 e^{-10}/100$. For $i=1,2,3$, put
\[
 A_i=Ae^{(2/\eps^2+(iK)^2)t_*},\qquad
 u_\eps(x,t)=
 \left(0,0,\left(A_i e^{-(2/\eps^2+(iK)^2)t}\sin(iKx)\right)_{i=1}^3\right).
\]
The initial amplitude norm is less than $3.754\times10^{-5}$,
well inside the $0.01$ tube, and decreases in time.
The nearest point on $m_-$ is zero, so $F(u_\eps)=|u_\eps|^2$;
hence this formula solves the actual linearized equation
$\partial_tu_\eps=\partial_{xx}u_\eps-2\eps^{-2}u_\eps$,
which is exactly (1.7) throughout its range. The boundary value
is zero. No author code or numerical PDE solver is used.

At $x_*=\pi/(4K)$, $t=t_*$, set $b=2/(\eps^2K^2)=1/50$ and
\[
 U=(1/\sqrt2,1,1/\sqrt2),\quad
 V_1=(1/\sqrt2,0,-3/\sqrt2),\quad
 W=((b+1)/\sqrt2,b+4,(b+9)/\sqrt2).
\]
Then $u=AU$, $u_x=AKV_1$ and $u_t=-AK^2W$ in the last three
coordinates. Writing $D_b=9b^2+64b+116$, exact Gram-matrix
calculation yields
\[
 |\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(V_1,W)}U|^2
       =2-\frac4{D_b}<2.
\]
Near $m_-$, $d_F(u)=|u|^2/\sqrt2$ and
$\nabla d_F=\sqrt2u$. Thus the literal (2.35) gradient $g_{\rm pr}$
has
\[
 |g_{\rm pr}|^2=4A^2-\frac{8A^2}{D_b}
     =4A^2\frac{288209}{293209},
\]
whereas $|\nabla d_F|^2=4A^2$.
The radial projection prescribed in the well tube has
$|\Pi_u u_x|^2=A^2K^2/2$, and therefore
\[
 |\psi_x|^2=2A^4K^2,\qquad
 |\Pi_u u_x|^2|g_{\rm pr}|^2
   =A^4K^2\left(2-\frac4{D_b}\right).
\]
This contradicts (2.41) if the unconditional (2.35) convention
is used there. It also directly disproves the asserted
classical coincidence of that projected definition.

The scope qualification is decisive: the actual text immediately
below (2.40) says to use the generalized differential when
$d_F$ is \emph{not} classically differentiable. With the
classical gradient at differentiability points, this example
no longer contradicts (2.41). That explicit later convention
was checked in the source image and is a local repair.
The example is not advanced as a counterexample to the
well-prepared limit theorem or to its integrated energy estimate.

Finally, differentiating (2.17) near the plus well gives
\[
 \nabla d_F(u)=-\sqrt2\,(u-P_{m_+}u),
\]
while near the minus well the sign is positive. The common
positive sign printed in (2.21) needs correction. Projection
onto the resulting line is unchanged by this sign.
State one consistent piecewise gradient convention, and correct
the sign and the classical-coincidence claim.

findings.complete_retained_argument_tex:
\subsection{P5: initial preparation permits remote small droplets
(Minor)}\label{P5}

\textbf{Location.}
Proposition 3.5, (3.28c), pp.~19--20, and the appeal to
Blaschke's theorem in its proof.

\textbf{Admissible initial-time counterexample.}
Let $d=3$, $\Omega=B_5(0)$, and let the prescribed interface
start at $\Sigma_0=\partial B_2(0)$ and follow
$\Sigma_t=\partial B_{\sqrt{4-4t}}(0)$ for a short time.
Use the compact two-circle wells from P1 and the closest
segment between $p_-$ and $p_+$, with a smooth optimal
transition profile. The outside boundary value is $p_-$,
which is an admissible smooth map into $m_-$.
A truncated optimal layer across $\Sigma_0$ gives
$E_\eps(0)=O(\eps^2)$ and $B(0)=O(\eps^2)$ when the bulk
phases are constant.

Add a second, plus-phase ball centered at $x_0=(3,0,0)$,
of radius $r_\eps=\sqrt\eps$, inside the minus phase.
Use the same smooth profile across this sphere, with thickness
of order $\eps$, and truncate its tails while staying away from
the principal interface and the outer boundary.
The calibration $\xi$ vanishes near the small ball. Its
additional energy and bulk error satisfy
\[
 E_{\eps,\mathrm{drop}}
  =O(r_\eps^2+\eps r_\eps+\eps^2)=O(\eps),\qquad
 B_{\mathrm{drop}}=O(r_\eps^3+\eps r_\eps^2)=O(\eps^{3/2}).
\]
Exponential tail errors do not change these bounds.
The values remain on the bounded closest segment. Consequently
the full preparation condition (1.15) holds with a uniform
constant. These are smooth compatible initial data for (1.7).

For every sufficiently small
$b_\eps\in[\eps^{1/6},2\eps^{1/6}]$, the level set
$\{\psi_\eps=c_F-b_\eps\}$ has a component around $x_0$.
Its displacement from the small sphere is
$O(\eps|\log\eps|)=o(r_\eps)$.
Points on this component remain a fixed positive distance
from $\Sigma_0$. No subsequence can satisfy the asserted
Hausdorff convergence at $t=0$.
At the same time, its extra perimeter is $O(\eps)$ and
its enclosed volume is $O(\eps^{3/2})$, fully consistent
with the perimeter and BV conclusions.

\textbf{Scope and repair.}
This is an initial-time counterexample under the stated
uniform preparation assumptions. It does not show a remote
droplet surviving to a fixed positive time: small droplets
may disappear rapidly. Blaschke compactness only supplies
some Hausdorff-convergent subsequence of compact sets; it
does not identify the limit from perimeter and $L^1$
convergence. Theorem 3.6 uses (3.28a)--(3.28b), and the
minimal-pair proof uses slice convergence, traces and Egorov's
theorem, rather than (3.28c). Removing that unused claim,
or replacing it by a separately proved positive-time
clearing statement, is a bounded repair.

findings.complete_retained_argument_tex:
\subsection{P6: normal-frame derivatives in higher codimension
(Minor)}\label{P6}

\textbf{Location.}
The normal-coordinate calculation (3.34)--(3.37), pp.~20--21,
used for (3.29b) and again in (4.10).

Let $q(s)=(\cos s,\sin s,0)$ and choose the smooth normal frame
\[
 \nu_1(s)=\cos s\,q(s)+\sin s\,e_3,\qquad
 \nu_2(s)=-\sin s\,q(s)+\cos s\,e_3.
\]
For fixed small $r>0$, set $u(s)=q(s)+r\nu_2(s)$.
The nearest point is $q(s)$ and the normal coordinate
$d_1(u(s))=\ip{u(s)-q(s)}{\nu_1(s)}$ vanishes identically.
But at $s=0$,
\[
 \frac{\dd}{\dd s}d_1(u(s))=0,\qquad
 \nu_1(0)\cdot u'(0)=-r\neq0.
\]
Thus the asserted gradient formula for individual normal
coordinates, and the claim that all derivatives of a normal
frame are tangential, fail in general codimension.
Translating the circle makes $0\in m_-$; a second distant
circle supplies the other well. The example is within a
smooth tubular neighborhood.

The required estimate can be proved without this false frame
identity. If $\nu_{\rm rad}=(u-P_mu)/|u-P_mu|$, then
$DP_m(u)\nu_{\rm rad}=0$, and smooth tube geometry gives
$\|DP_m(u)\|\leq1+C\delta_0$. Hence
\[
 |\partial_iP_m(u)|
 \leq(1+C\delta_0)
     |\partial_i u-\Pi_{\rm rad}\partial_i u|.
\]
This supplies the bounded projection estimate used later.
Correcting the normal connection, or using this
coordinate-free proof, avoids a loss in the essential
energy bound.

retained_calculation.analytic_conclusion: The claimed gradient of the normal coordinate omits the normal connection. DP_m annihilates the radial normal and supplies the needed bounded repair.

\subsection{P7: curvature extension through its cutoff annulus
(Minor)}\label{P7}

\textbf{Location.}
The first identity in (2.31), p.~10, compared with (2.30).

For a circle or sphere of nonzero mean curvature, the extended
curvature field has the form
$H(x)=\kappa(P_{\Sigma_t}x)\eta_0(x)n(x)$.
Choose an admissible radial cutoff, equal to one for
$|d_\Sigma|\leq\delta_0$ and zero for
$|d_\Sigma|\geq2\delta_0$.
On a normal ray,
\[
 (n\cdot\nabla)H=\kappa\,\eta_0'(d_\Sigma)n.
\]
The derivative is nonzero somewhere in the cutoff annulus.
For the flat switch $s$ from P1, choose a smooth $\chi(r)$
equal to one for $r\leq7a/4$ and zero for $r\geq15a/8$.
Set $\eta_0(r)=[1-s((r-a)/a)]\chi(r)$ for $a<r<2a$,
extend by one for $0\leq r\leq a$, then evenly.
Its support lies strictly inside $(-2a,2a)$, as required
by (2.29), while $\eta_0'(3a/2)=-2/a$ is unchanged.
Thus the unrestricted normal derivative identity cannot hold
throughout $B_{2\delta_0}(\Sigma_t)$.

On the smaller tube where $\eta_0=1$, the normal derivative
does vanish. Since $\xi$ is supported in that smaller tube,
$(\xi\cdot\nabla)H=0$ remains valid everywhere it is needed.
The appendix uses this contracted relation. Restrict the
first identity's domain and retain the contracted identity.

retained_calculation.analytic_conclusion: The unrestricted normal derivative identity fails in the cutoff annulus; its xi-contracted version remains valid.

\subsection{P8: derivative of the negative part (Minor)}\label{P8}

\textbf{Location.}
The displayed calculation (3.13), p.~16, with the definitions
immediately preceding it.

The convention is the positive-valued negative part
$z^-=\max\{-z,0\}$. Away from the interface and where
$0<\psi_\eps<c_F$, the function
\[
 w_\eps=c_F\chi-c_F+2(\psi_\eps-c_F)^-
        =c_F\chi+c_F-2\psi_\eps
\]
satisfies $\partial_iw_\eps=-2\partial_i\psi_\eps$.
The printed plus sign is incorrect.
A nonconstant monotone optimal profile at a point strictly
inside one phase has $\partial_i\psi_\eps\neq0$ and
$\eta(d_\Sigma)\neq0$, so the discrepancy is realized by
smooth admissible local data, rather than only at the
nondifferentiable threshold.

The subsequent estimates use absolute values and Young's
inequality. Correcting this sign leaves those bounds
available. Also, the positive-part auxiliary
$(\psi_\eps-c_F)^+$ is identically zero for the bounded
phase distance used here; introducing it is redundant but
is not itself a mathematical defect.

\subsection{P9: the bulk-energy coefficient in (5.40) (Minor)}
\label{P9}

\textbf{Location.}
Equations (5.39)--(5.40), p.~31.

Use smooth well-valued bulk maps that are constant near
$\Sigma_0$, satisfy the same-angle minimal-pair condition
for the parallel circles in P2, and are nonconstant only
on a compact subset of one bulk region outside
$B_{2\delta}(\Sigma_0)$. For example, take a nonconstant
smooth compactly supported angle function in the plus
bulk and the zero angle elsewhere. These data avoid the
trace-regularity problem in P2 altogether.

Let $R=\sum_\pm\int_{\Omega_0^\pm}|\nabla u_0^\pm|^2>0$.
The construction is the exact original bulk map on the
support of those gradients, where $F=0$ and $\nabla\psi=0$.
Its contribution to $E_\eps/\eps$ is exactly $R/2$.
The optimal normal layer contributes $O(\eps)$ after this
division, and the truncated tails tend to zero exponentially.
Thus
\[
 \lim_{\eps\downarrow0}\frac{E_\eps[u_\eps^{\rm in}|\Sigma_0]}{\eps}
    =\frac12\sum_\pm\int_{\Omega_0^\pm}
                  |\nabla u_0^\pm|^2
    =\frac R2,
\]
whereas (5.40) prints the sum without the factor $1/2$.
This is also the coefficient carried by the preceding
formula (5.39). Restoring it does not alter the $O(\eps)$
preparation estimate.

findings.complete_retained_argument_tex:
\subsection{P10: zero spatial gradient in the final square completion
(Minor)}\label{P10}

\textbf{Location.}
The zero convention in (2.39a), p.~11, and the final
square-completion step on p.~35 leading to (A.2a), p.~33.

Write $g=\partial d_F(u_\eps)$ and $c=\Div\xi$.
Immediately before its last square, the proof contains
\[
 c^2|g|^2+2\eps c\,\nabla\psi_\eps\cdot H
             +\eps^2|\Pi_{u_\eps}\nabla u_\eps|^2|H|^2.
\]
It replaces this by
$|c|g|n_\eps+\eps|\Pi_{u_\eps}\nabla u_\eps|H|^2$.
Where $\nabla\psi_\eps=0$, the printed convention is
$n_\eps=0$. If $g\neq0$ and
$\Pi_{u_\eps}\nabla u_\eps=0$, the first expression is
$c^2|g|^2$ and the proposed square is zero. The chain rule
does not remove that discrepancy.

These pointwise data are compatible with smooth prepared
initial data. Start with a truncated optimal layer and
choose a small fixed open patch $U$ in the minus side of
the calibration collar, away from the actual layer, where
$\Div\xi\neq0$. For the parallel circles in P2, take the
closest segment to be vertical and add the smooth
perturbation $\eps\zeta e_3$ to the constant minus phase,
where $\zeta=1$ on $U$ and is supported in that side of
the collar. For small $\eps$, this adds $O(\eps)$ to the
energy and $O(\eps^2)$ to the bulk error, and changes no
outer boundary value. On $U$ at $t=0$,
\[
 u_\eps=\eps e_3,\quad \nabla u_\eps=0,\quad
 F=\eps^2,\quad g=\sqrt2\eps e_3,\quad
 \partial_tu_\eps=-2\eps^{-1}e_3.
\]
The omitted term after division by $2\eps$ is
$\eps(\Div\xi)^2>0$.

\emph{Precise scope.} This establishes a defect in the
unconditional algebraic completion, with an admissible
smooth initial plateau. It is not claimed to construct a
fixed positive-time plateau or to refute an almost-everywhere
interior-time version of Lemma A.2. Such a stronger assertion
would require additional analysis.

A bounded correction is explicit. Choose an arbitrary
\emph{unit} normal where $\nabla\psi_\eps=0$, as in
Fischer--Laux--Simon \cite{FLS}, (11a), or retain the omitted
nonnegative remainder. On that zero-gradient set,
\[
 \frac{c^2|g|^2}{2\eps}
 \leq \|\Div\xi\|_\infty^2\,\frac{F(u_\eps)}{\eps}
 \leq C\left(\frac{\eps}{2}|\nabla u_\eps|^2+
                    \frac{F(u_\eps)}{\eps}
                    -\xi\cdot\nabla\psi_\eps\right).
\]
Thus the remainder is controlled by $E_\eps$ and does not
by itself refute Proposition 2.9. The three-square estimate
on p.~36 should also use a generic constant (for example
the usual factor $3$), rather than coefficient one; that
constant is absorbed in the same estimate.
